opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and it's one we think about a lot. The honest answer is that it's become much more of a structured, data-driven process than it was in the early days.

When we look at a new city, the first thing we try to understand is how different it really is from what we've already seen. A lot of driving is universal: lanes, intersections, pedestrians, cyclists, other cars negotiating right of way. Our system has driven tens of millions of fully autonomous miles across places like Phoenix, San Francisco, and Los Angeles, so there's a large core of behavior that transfers well. The question is what's in the tail: local road geometry, unusual signage, different traffic norms, weather, how aggressive or polite drivers tend to be, the mix of agents on the road.

So we typically go in, drive the area, collect data, and run it through our evaluation pipeline. We replay the new data through simulation, look at where the system's performance metrics differ from our established baselines, and see whether issues cluster into categories we already handle well or whether genuinely new phenomena show up. That tells us whether we mostly need validation, or whether there's real modeling work to do.

One thing that's been very encouraging is that as our models have gotten larger and more general, especially with more learned, foundation-model-style components, generalization to new places has improved a lot. When we've gone to new cities, the system often performs surprisingly well out of the box, and the remaining work is more about the long tail and building a rigorous safety case for that specific operating domain.

That last part is key. Even if the driving looks good, we have a high bar for demonstrating safety before removing the driver. So a lot of the work is validation: making sure we've covered the scenarios that matter locally, that our simulation is realistic for that environment, and that the statistical evidence holds up. Things like snow, or very different road cultures in international markets, are where we expect more effort, and we invest in those deliberately rather than assuming everything transfers.

So it's a mix: measure the gap carefully, lean on generalization where it holds, and do targeted work on whatever is truly new.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a question we think about constantly, because the whole point of what we've been building is a driver that generalizes, not one that's tuned to a single city. So the way I'd frame it is that every new environment has some mix of things we've already seen and things that are genuinely new, and the work is really about figuring out where that boundary sits.

When we go into a new city, the first thing we do is drive it, collect data, and look at where the distribution differs from what we've trained on. Some of that is obvious. Phoenix has very wide, structured roads and almost no weather. San Francisco has steep hills, dense pedestrians, double-parked vehicles everywhere, fog. Los Angeles has a lot of freeway and a different driving culture. Austin and Atlanta bring their own flavors. But a lot of it is subtle: how people signal, how aggressive merges are, what the local road markings and signage conventions look like, how construction zones get set up. Those are the things that don't show up until you're actually there.

The encouraging part is that each new city has been requiring less bespoke work than the one before it. Because the system is largely learned end to end at this point, with large models for perception, prediction, and behavior that are trained on an enormous and diverse corpus, most of the behaviors transfer. We're not rewriting rules for every intersection type. What we're really doing is validating. We run the driver, we find the long-tail cases where it's uncertain or behaves suboptimally, we feed those back into training, and we test in simulation at a scale we could never achieve on the road. Simulation is a huge part of this, because we can take real scenarios from a new city and perturb them, create variations, and stress the system before any rider ever sits in the car.

Then there's the safety case, which is a separate but related piece. Before we launch without a driver in a new place, we need statistical confidence that performance meets our bar, and we need to understand the specific risk profile of that environment. That takes miles, both real and simulated, and it takes a very careful readiness review.

So I'd say the additional work is less about teaching the car to drive again and more about discovering the gaps, closing them, and proving to ourselves that we've closed them. And honestly, the trend line is what matters to me. If each new city is faster than the last, that tells you the generalization is real.

astra-6.text:
We look at what’s actually different about the environment. A new city may have different road layouts, traffic patterns, or behaviors that we need to understand. Weather can introduce another set of challenges. So it’s less about the geographic distance from where we already operate and more about the kinds of situations the driver will encounter.

The key question is how well our existing capabilities generalize. We can evaluate that through testing and simulation, identify gaps, and then do targeted work to address them. Some differences may require additional training data; others may require changes to the system. Before launching, we need evidence that the system can handle the conditions within the area where we intend to operate safely and reliably.

sol-6.1.text:
We look at what’s actually different about the environment. Is it a new road layout, a different kind of interaction with other road users, or weather that we haven’t had to handle before? A lot of the underlying driving capabilities transfer, so going to a new city doesn’t mean starting from scratch. But we need to understand where that transfer works well and where there are gaps.

We collect data in the new environment and use it to evaluate the system, both on the road and in simulation. When we find a challenging situation, we can turn it into a test and use that to guide improvements. The amount of additional work depends much more on the novelty and difficulty of those situations than on the number of miles of road. Ultimately, the question is whether we have sufficient evidence that the system can operate safely within the area and conditions where we intend to launch.
